comparator.name: Regenerative Medicine and Technology (BSc)
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–2027 regulations set a 150 EC major and a 30 EC minor. The first two years combine courses with continuing work in laboratory skills, design and academic development. The example uses the 7 EC clinical design project. Year 3 has a 30 EC minor and a 30 EC graduation project combining an internship, an individual thesis and an oral defence. The previous year’s course guide provides context for the named courses retained in the current regulations.

routeSelection.basis: The current regulations list two 7 EC options for the Year 2 design project. The example uses the Clinical Track, listed first in Appendix 3. The rest of the degree is shared.

core: Biological and molecular foundations of regenerative medicine: biochemistry and the chemistry of life, cell biology, tissue structure and function, stem-cell potency and cell-matrix interaction (The Molecular Basis of Life; Cells: From Lab to Production)

Medical foundations: anatomy, physiology and immunology of the organ systems targeted by regenerative medicine, inflammation, foreign-body response and transplant immunology, wound healing and vascularisation (Principles of Medicine; Technological Trends in Regenerative Medicine)

Regeneration and tissue repair: the intrinsic regenerative capacity of tissues, functional repair versus regeneration, ageing, and cell-based, immune-based and gene-based regenerative therapies (The Intrinsic Regenerative Capacity of the Human Body; Technological Trends in Regenerative Medicine)

Engineering, physics and mathematics foundations: vectors, differential equations, mechanics of materials, rheology, thermodynamics, circuits, and the chemistry and materials science needed to design biomedical materials (Foundations of Engineering; Materials Science in Biological Applications)

Advanced regeneration technologies: biomaterials, tissue engineering, micro- and nanofabrication, microfluidics, organs-on-chips and biofabrication (Materials Science in Biological Applications; Advanced Technologies for Regeneration)

Programming, statistics, data analysis and computational modelling: scripting, probability, regression, data-driven and differential-equation modelling and an introduction to neural networks (Coding and Data Crunching; Data Analysis & Modelling of Biosystems)
Laboratory skills and biomedical laboratory research: lab skills lines in years 1 and 2, experimental design, statistics for experimental data and reporting

Design, innovation and entrepreneurship: the design project lines (analysing a clinical problem, designing and marketing a new application), valorisation and market value, and the ethics of regenerative medicine applications
Academic development: self-regulated learning, professional behaviour, scientific storytelling, personal development and ethical and scientific-integrity standards (Academic Development Lines)
Research training and thesis: a 20-week individual graduation project with thesis and oral defence, preceded by a 30-EC minor
adjacent: Biomedical engineering and medical devices: engineering combined with medicine for devices and implants, with medical-device developer as a named career and biomedical engineering and imaging engineering as named further study
questions: How can the body's own repair ability be stimulated or engineered so that damaged tissue is regenerated as an alternative to organ transplantation or life-long medication?
How are scientific discoveries in regenerative medicine turned into treatments, products and ventures that reach patients?

trace: introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function and connects them to health and disease; it directly implements the biological foundation that The Molecular Basis of Life and Principles of Medicine build on, without their regenerative-medicine framing
Develops molecular cell biology through signalling, cell division, tissue organisation, cell fate and stem cells. This supplies foundations for regenerative cell biology and cell-production study.

studies the normal functioning of the human body, from molecular and cellular physiology through homeostasis and signalling to the integration of organ systems; it directly implements the physiology taught in Principles of Medicine

explores the chemistry of life, namely proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids, metabolic pathways and applications in medicine and biotechnology; it directly implements the biomolecular and chemical part of The Molecular Basis of Life, but it is biochemistry rather than the general, organic and physical chemistry that course also teaches

introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work on blood, bacteria, protein production and analysis, DNA isolation and bioinformatics searches and builds a foundation for biomedical research; it directly implements part of the laboratory training in the lab skills lines, although its themes do not include stem-cell culture or biomaterials work

Studies cell injury, inflammation, tissue repair, regeneration and fibrosis, plus gene-based therapies and cell manipulation. It directly supports the biological study of repair and parts of advanced therapy.

studies the structure of the human body in relation to function through imaging, surface anatomy and dissection materials, system by system; it directly implements the anatomy taught in Principles of Medicine

covers the origin, kinetics, targets, therapeutic use and toxicity of drugs and explains therapies through molecular targets and physiological consequences; it makes a specific complementary contribution to understanding the medicinal and advanced-therapy treatments that regenerative approaches complement or replace, but it contains no regenerative-medicine content

teaches innate and adaptive immune responses, recognition of self and non-self, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology; it directly implements the immunology and inflammation taught in Principles of Medicine and the immune interactions that Technological Trends in Regenerative Medicine applies to implants and cell therapies, although it is not taught in a transplant or regeneration context
Examines organ-system pathology and treatment, including renal failure, dialysis and transplantation. It supplies clinical context for regeneration and alternatives to transplantation.

provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling and applies them to a case study; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the physics, mathematics and materials foundations of Foundations of Engineering, although it is framed for sustainability and not for human biomechanics

builds on Sustainability Essentials I with three topics, waves, chemistry and materials science, and a project that applies them; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the chemistry and materials-science foundations behind Materials Science in Biological Applications, but it is a sustainability course and teaches no biomaterials or cell-material interaction

introduces structured and object-oriented programming in Python with testing and debugging and computational problem-solving; it directly implements the scripting and programming foundation of Coding and Data Crunching, which uses R

teaches integration, complex numbers, differential equations and equation solving; it directly implements the mathematics of differential equations and integration used in Foundations of Engineering and Data Analysis & Modelling of Biosystems

develops data visualisation, cleaning and manipulation on real data sets and ends with an own research project; it directly implements the data-handling, visualisation and analysis part of Coding and Data Crunching

provides the foundation of mathematical statistics: probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; it directly implements the probability and statistics taught in Coding and Data Crunching at greater mathematical depth

teaches numerical methods for differential equations, root finding, interpolation, differentiation and integration with attention to accuracy and stability; it directly implements the differential-equation modelling and simulation of Data Analysis & Modelling of Biosystems, but without biological applications
Trains predictive modelling, resampling, classification, regularisation and tree methods. These are transferable data-driven methods for biosystem modelling.

teaches the design and development cycle in a team (interviewing customers, forming a product concept, developing a fabrication method, analysing costs and sustainability) with experiments, mathematical modelling and prototyping; it directly implements the team design-and-development cycle of the design project lines, although the products are consumer products and not clinical applications

teaches venture creation from ideation to pitch with design thinking, business-model development, market validation and business planning; it directly implements the entrepreneurship and market-value part of the curriculum (From Research to Market Value and the valorisation aims of the design project), without any health-care content

teaches how to plan and carry out customer and market research, analyse the findings and turn them into business ideas; it makes a specific complementary contribution to testing the market value of an innovation, but it is not specific to health care

teaches research design, operationalisation, sampling, experiments and surveys and descriptive and inferential statistics including analysis of variance; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the experimental design, statistics and reporting of experimental data in the lab skills lines and to research training for the thesis, although it is oriented to business and behavioural research

teaches moral-reasoning theories and practical ethics including privacy, equality and future generations; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the ethical debate on regenerative-medicine applications in Regenerative Medicine in Society and to the ethical and integrity standards of the academic development lines, but it has no biomedical focus

alternatives.label: Biomedical Science, Engineering Foundations and Innovation
alternatives.labelReason: Study the biology of disease and tissue repair through cell biology, biochemistry, physiology, immunology and lab work. Add mathematics, materials science, data analysis, product design and entrepreneurship. Maastricht provides more specialised training in cell therapies, biomaterials, tissue engineering and fabrication.
alternatives.concept: Study the biology of disease and tissue repair through cell biology, biochemistry, physiology, immunology and lab work. Add mathematics, materials science, data analysis, product design and entrepreneurship. Maastricht provides more specialised training in cell therapies, biomaterials, tissue engineering and fabrication.
progression: Foundations of Life Science precedes cell biology, lab work and anatomy. Cell biology and physiology precede molecular pathology and organ-system disease. Programming, mathematical methods and introductory data analysis precede machine learning. Sustainability Essentials I precedes Sustainability Essentials II. Entrepreneurship precedes market research. Consumer Product Design uses the planned final spring term.

selection.assessment: One plan combines biomedical science, laboratory work, engineering foundations and healthcare innovation context. A second device-focused plan could use robotics, signal processing, numerical modelling and physiology, with materials and prototyping. These courses add sensing, control and mechanical modelling, but the catalogue offers limited dedicated study of device design, biomechanics and clinical testing. The material and fabrication direction has complementary chemistry, polymer properties, spectroscopy and sustainable materials design, and cell biology includes stem cells. There is insufficient dedicated work in cell–material interaction, tissue scaffolds, cell manufacture or biofabrication to sustain that direction separately.

blocks: Biochemistry, cell biology and laboratory skills
Both study the molecular basis of life. UCR focuses on proteins, metabolism and biochemical techniques. Maastricht also uses chemistry and cell biology to introduce regenerative medicine.
Both develop cell biology, including cell fate and stem cells. Maastricht extends this to cell sourcing, manufacture and cell–material constructs.
Both develop molecular laboratory skills. Maastricht also integrates lab practice across its first-year courses.
Maastricht awards 2 EC for meeting the first-year laboratory attendance requirement.
Maastricht continues lab training in cell culture, assays and materials. UCR develops related laboratory foundations in its life science lab.
Maastricht awards 2 EC for meeting the second-year laboratory attendance requirement.
Anatomy, physiology, immunology, disease and tissue repair
Both study organ function and physiology. Maastricht combines physiology with anatomy and immunology in the same course.
Both examine immune responses relevant to regenerative treatments. Maastricht also studies therapies and devices, including implants and cell-based treatments.
Both study tissue repair and regeneration. Maastricht concentrates on the regenerative capacity of different tissues and the factors that limit it.
Maastricht introduces regenerative medicine and its applications in society. UCR covers related biology and general ethics across separate courses.
Engineering, physics, chemistry and materials foundations
Both develop quantitative and physical foundations. UCR includes mechanics and material properties in sustainability contexts. Maastricht also teaches engineering tools for biomechanics.
UCR studies material properties and characterisation in sustainability. Maastricht focuses on biomaterials and their interaction with cells.
Maastricht teaches specialist methods such as microfabrication, microfluidics, organs-on-chips and biofabrication.
Programming, statistics, data analysis and modelling
Both use programming to explore and analyse data. Maastricht’s course combines R scripting and statistics in regenerative-medicine examples.
Both develop data-driven models. Maastricht combines these with differential equations and examples from biological systems.
Both develop and test product concepts in teams. Maastricht uses a clinical regeneration problem. UCR uses consumer products.
Both explore how ideas become marketable products. Maastricht focuses on the value of regenerative-medicine research. UCR teaches general venture design and validation.
Maastricht introduces the design process through interviews, journal clubs, visits and a project pitch.
Academic skills, research methods, minor and bachelor thesis
Both develop academic, communication and reflective skills. Maastricht continues its academic development sequence throughout the year.
Maastricht continues its academic development sequence and prepares students for their minor and graduation project.
Students complete a 30 EC minor. Choices can include courses at Maastricht or another university, with approval where required.
Maastricht’s 30 EC graduation project combines an internship, an individual thesis and an oral defence. UCR’s optional independent research is outside the scheduled plan.

notes.text: Both plans study biochemistry, cell biology, physiology and data analysis. Maastricht adds specialist work in cell manufacture, biomaterials, gene and cell therapies, microfabrication and clinical design. UCR combines biomedical science with related engineering foundations and product design.

Maastricht combines courses with continuing lab, design and academic development work. In the final year, students take a 30 EC minor and complete a 30 EC graduation project. UCR’s optional independent research is separate from the scheduled courses.

audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht’s Regenerative Medicine and Technology bachelor combines biology, medicine and engineering to study ways to repair or regenerate tissues.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The 2026–2027 example uses Maastricht’s clinical design project. The UCR plan combines biomedical science with data analysis, engineering foundations and innovation.
